title: Tarte Tatin
subtitle: Upside-down caramelised apple tart
excerpt: Apples cooked in butter and caramel until deeply golden, covered with a circle of pastry, baked, and then inverted onto a plate to reveal the caramelised apple surface. The most famous of all French tarts.
sourceNotes: Tarte Tatin was created accidentally by Caroline (or Stéphanie) Tatin at the Hotel Tatin in Lamotte-Beuvron in the Sologne, probably in the 1880s. The story goes that one of the sisters began making a classic tarte aux pommes but left the apples cooking in butter and sugar for too long; to rescue the situation she placed the pastry on top and put the tin in the oven, inverting it when done. Auguste Escoffier helped popularise the recipe in Paris after the Hotel Tatin's restaurant was brought to his attention. The Société des Amis de la Tarte Tatin maintains the original recipe in Lamotte-Beuvron.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tarte tatin is best served 30 minutes to 1 hour after baking, warm with cream or crème fraîche. It can be made up to 4 hours ahead and gently rewarmed in a 150°C oven for 10 minutes before inverting.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sugar heated until it melts and turns golden to dark amber, developing deep, slightly bitter sweetness. For tarte Tatin, the caramel forms around the apples as they cook in butter and sugar; it continues to develop in the oven and becomes the sauce when the tart is inverted.

content.text: Tarte Tatin is made in an ovenproof frying pan or cast-iron skillet: apples are cooked in butter and sugar directly in the pan until the

begins to form, then covered with a disc of pastry and finished in the oven. The pastry bakes while the apples continue to caramelise below it. Inverting the tart reveals the apple surface glazed in dark caramel. The inversion requires confidence, a hesitant flip is a ruined tart.

items.prepNote: about 6 large, Granny Smith or Cox, peeled, cored, halved
ready-made, or home-made (200 g flour + 100 g butter + 1 egg yolk)

content.text: Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Toss the apple halves with the lemon juice. In the 26 cm cast-iron skillet, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the sugar in an even layer. Cook without stirring until the sugar begins to caramelise at the edges, about 5 to 7 minutes.

Arrange the apple halves tightly in the caramel, cut-side up, packing them as closely as possible, they will shrink. Cook over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes until the caramel turns a deep amber and the apples have softened and are sitting in a dark, reduced caramel. The apples should be very golden.
Roll the pastry to a circle slightly larger than the pan. Lay it over the apples, tucking the edges down the inside of the pan around the apples.
Transfer to the oven and bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is golden brown.

Remove from the oven and allow to rest for 15 minutes, this helps the caramel set slightly so it does not pour off immediately when inverted. Place a large plate over the pan and, holding both firmly, flip in one confident, fast movement. Lift the pan away. Any apple that has stuck can be repositioned. Serve warm.

items.symptom: The caramel is too liquid when the tart is inverted
items.cause: The apples released a lot of juice, thinning the caramel. The resting period was too short.
items.fix: Always rest for 15 minutes before inverting. If the caramel still looks very liquid, return the pan to the hob over high heat for 3 to 4 minutes to reduce before resting and inverting.

items.symptom: The apples are undercooked and firm
items.cause: They were not cooked long enough in the caramel on the hob before going into the oven.
items.fix: The apples should be very soft and deeply golden before the pastry goes on. If firm, continue cooking on the hob for a further 5 to 10 minutes before adding the pastry.

items.symptom: The pastry is still pale after 30 minutes
items.cause: The oven was not properly preheated, or the skillet blocked the heat from reaching the pastry surface.
items.fix: Increase to 210°C and continue for 10 minutes. The pastry needs to be properly golden before the tart is ready.

content.text: The Hotel Tatin in Lamotte-Beuvron is still there and still serves the tart. The Sologne is flat, forested country between Orléans and Blois, apple and game territory, which explains the filling. Auguste Escoffier and the food writer Curnonsky brought the recipe to Paris in the early 20th century. It is now the best-known French tart outside France and has inspired many other upside-down fruit tarts.
